newsitem.title: UK: Euro products outlook - gas oil strong, margin firm.
newsitem.headline: Euro products outlook - gas oil strong, margin firm.

text.p: European gas oil may extend its rally this week, gasoline and fuel oil should remain steady, but jet may come under selling pressure, traders said. While the outlook was mixed, a trading manager at a major oil company expected the strength in gas oil to drive typical refining margins up 50 cents in the next few weeks to $2.50 per barrel.
"Demand is very, very strong for all grades of gas oil," he said. "It seems end-users are scared by the fact that gas oil could be even higher in a couple of weeks."

Gasoline was well-supported after several hundred thousand tonnes were sold to the U.S. in the past few days, he said, but a weak reforming margin meant unleaded 98 octane was in short supply and lower octane was weak.
"Now the market in 98 octane is tightening because the reforming margin has decreased so refiners have reduced platformer throughput," a refiner said.
"We expect a widening of the 98 and 95 octane spread."
Jet fuel, currently at five-year highs, was at tank tops throughout Europe, traders said, and premiums were on the way down as Caribbean cargoes headed to Europe.
End-users had stocked up after the tension in Iraq three weeks ago, but this and an open arbitrage window meant premiums were vulnerable to a modest sell-off.
The predicted 50 cent rise in refining margins would imply a $1.50 jump in the gas oil/Brent crack, from $6.50 to $8.00 per barrel, the major trading manager said.
France, Germany, UK, Ireland, Turkey, Syria, Lebanon and Greece were all singled out as gas oil demand hot-spots.
Even 400,000 tonnes of U.S. imports this month, equivalent to two percent of demand, hardly dampened sentiment.
One dealer said the U.S. imports only replaced a fall in Russian exports during September. Ventspils gas oil exports were 30 percent below normal this month, he added.
Traders did not expect the transatlantic arbitrage to Europe to stay open long because U.S. stocks were already low.
He said low stocks in the U.S. and Germany would continue to exert upwards pressure on 0.2 while France and Germany continue to import large amounts of diesel.
"Low sulphur diesel will not go alot higher than $10 premium to high sulphur, but both grades could continue to strengthen," a trader said.
We could see 0.2 premiums in double figures when October futures go off the board," he added.

Fuel oil demand was expected to ease, but limited supply gave some support. High sulphur cracked fuel was expected to stay around $106-108 fob in both NWE and the Med, with the Med with more potential to rise than the north.
"I see it as flat, unlikely to dip lower because there remains some tightness, but also lacking the fundamentals to move much higher," said one dealer of the NWE.
